subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Section A: The 19th century novel (closed book)
Section B: The modern prose text
Reading and responding to prose: Assessment Objectives and terminology

questions.q: In Section A, the 19th century novel is assessed 'closed book'. What does this mean?
options: Students may not take a copy of the novel into the examination
Students answer only multiple-choice questions on the novel
Students may bring an annotated copy of the novel into the exam
The novel is read aloud to students during the exam
questions.explain: 'Closed book' means the text is not available in the exam, so responses rely on memory.

questions.q: The 19th century, in which the Section A novels were written, covers which years?
questions.explain: The 19th century runs from 1800 to 1899.

questions.q: In Section B, a 'modern prose text' is a work of prose fiction from which period?
options: The 20th or 21st century
The medieval period
The early 18th century
The Renaissance
questions.explain: Modern prose texts are drawn from the 20th and 21st centuries.

questions.q: Which skill is assessed by Assessment Objective 1 (AO1)?
options: Responding to texts and supporting ideas with references and quotations
Analysing a writer's use of language and structure
Showing understanding of historical context
Using accurate spelling and punctuation
questions.explain: AO1 rewards an informed personal response supported by textual references and quotations.

questions.q: Assessment Objective 2 (AO2) requires students to do what?
options: Analyse the language, form and structure a writer uses to create meaning
Recall the plot of the novel in detail
Compare two unseen poems
Write about the author's biography
questions.explain: AO2 focuses on how writers use language, form and structure, using subject terminology.

questions.q: Assessment Objective 3 (AO3) is concerned with what?
options: The relationship between a text and the context in which it was written
The accuracy of a student's punctuation
The number of quotations a student can memorise
The length of the student's answer
questions.explain: AO3 assesses understanding of the contexts in which texts were written and received.

questions.q: A narrator who tells the story using 'I' and 'me' is using which narrative perspective?
options: First-person narration
Third-person omniscient narration
Second-person narration
Third-person limited narration
questions.explain: First-person narration uses 'I' and tells events from within the narrator's own viewpoint.

questions.q: What is the term for the central character around whom a novel's action revolves?
options: The protagonist
The antagonist
The narrator
The author
questions.explain: The protagonist is the main character whose actions drive the story.

questions.q: A third-person 'omniscient' narrator is one who does what?
options: Knows the thoughts and feelings of all the characters
Is a character taking part in the events
Only knows what one character sees and thinks
Speaks directly to the reader as 'you'
questions.explain: An omniscient narrator has all-knowing access to every character's inner life.

questions.q: Why is understanding social and historical context (AO3) especially useful when studying a 19th century novel?
options: It helps explain the attitudes, values and conditions that shaped the characters and events
It allows students to bring the book into the exam
It removes the need to use quotations
It is the only objective assessed in Section A
questions.explain: Context illuminates the Victorian values and social conditions that shape the text.

questions.q: A key difference a student might explore between a modern prose text and a 19th century novel is that the modern text...
options: Often reflects more recent social concerns and language
Never uses figurative language
Must be non-fiction
Cannot have a narrator
questions.explain: Modern prose typically engages contemporary issues and uses more recent forms of language.

questions.q: Dramatic irony occurs when what happens?
options: The reader knows something that a character does not
Two characters have the same name
The novel is set in the past
A chapter ends without resolution
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises when the reader's knowledge exceeds a character's, creating tension.

questions.q: Foreshadowing is a technique in which a writer does what?
options: Hints at events that will happen later in the story
Summarises the whole plot at the start of the novel
Describes a setting in great detail
Uses only first-person narration
questions.explain: Foreshadowing plants clues that anticipate later developments in the narrative.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a 'theme' of a novel?
options: A central idea or message explored throughout the text, such as loyalty or ambition
The sequence of events that make up the story
The place and time in which the story is set
The person telling the story
questions.explain: A theme is a recurring idea or message developed across the whole text.

questions.q: 'Characterisation' refers to the ways in which a writer does what?
options: Creates and develops characters through their speech, actions and description
Divides a novel into chapters
Sets the story in a particular historical period
Ends a chapter on a moment of tension
questions.explain: Characterisation is how a writer builds and reveals characters through what they say, do and are described as.

questions.q: Because Section A is closed book, an effective revision strategy is to do what?
options: Memorise a bank of key quotations to support points in the exam
Plan to bring detailed notes into the examination
Avoid learning any quotations
Focus only on the modern prose text
questions.explain: Without the text in the exam, learned quotations are essential to evidence points (AO1).

questions.q: A student writes: 'The writer uses the metaphor of a "cage" to suggest the character feels trapped by society.' Which Assessment Objective is this student mainly demonstrating?
options: AO2 - analysing language and its effects
AO1 - maintaining a personal response
AO3 - understanding context
AO4 - spelling and punctuation
questions.explain: Analysing the effect of a specific language device (the metaphor) is AO2 work.

questions.q: A student explains how rigid Victorian class distinctions influence how a character is treated in a 19th century novel. Which Assessment Objective is being met?
options: AO3 - understanding the context in which the text was written
AO2 - analysing structure
AO1 - using quotations
AO4 - accurate written expression
questions.explain: Linking the text to Victorian social conditions demonstrates contextual understanding (AO3).

questions.q: To support a point about a character's kindness, a student embeds a brief, well-chosen quotation into their sentence. This most directly demonstrates which objective?
options: AO1 - supporting interpretations with textual references
AO2 - analysing form
AO3 - discussing context
AO4 - sentence accuracy
questions.explain: Using apt quotation to back up an interpretation is a core AO1 skill.

questions.q: In a modern prose text, a retrospective narrator says: 'If I had known then what I know now...' This is an example of which technique?
options: Foreshadowing, hinting that something significant is to come
Dramatic irony between two characters
Third-person omniscient narration
Onomatopoeia
questions.explain: The narrator's comment signals that important events lie ahead, which is foreshadowing.

specSource: CCEA GCSE English Literature (2017) specification; Unit 1: The Study of Prose
